batches.label: Week One
batches.title: Week One Build Plan
batches.intro:
The order matters less than the dependencies. Tickets 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 don't depend on anything else — start any of those on day one. Ticket 4 needs 1 and 2 finished first. Ticket 8 needs 7. Ticket 9 needs 1. Ticket 10 is last — it's the one that connects everything to the real backend instead of placeholder data.

Each ticket below has the same shape: what you're building in plain language, why it exists, then the technical spec — files, implementation notes, a definition of done, and a command or step to prove it works.

Tick the checkbox on a ticket once it's done. Your progress is saved on this device.

batches.label: Batch Two
batches.title: Batch Two Build Plan
batches.intro:
Pairs: 11 with 16, 12 with 17, 13 with 18, 14 with 19, 15 with 20. Frontend can start immediately against the planned responses and switch to the real API when its backend partner is done. Do 11 first, since nothing runs without the database.

Each ticket says what you will see working, then the files, the approach, a definition of done and a check. Tick a box when finished; progress saves on this device.

tickets.title: Syllabus tables and seed the Python syllabus
tickets.summary: Before a user can be "placed" into a syllabus, a syllabus has to exist in the database. This ticket builds the two tables that hold it: one for the big levels (Beginner, Elementary, Intermediate, Advanced) and one for the topics inside each level.
tickets.why: Everything else this week — the diagnostic result, the results screen, the browse page — points at these rows. Build this first.
tickets.how: Add two tables. syllabus_levels: id, order, title, description. syllabus_topics: id, levelId (points at a level), order, title, blurb, conceptSlug. Seed four levels — Beginner, Elementary, Intermediate, Advanced — and spread your six existing concepts (variables-and-types, control-flow, functions, data-structures, oop, exception-handling) across them in a sensible order. Follow the same id and timestamp style already used elsewhere in the schema.
dod: The migration runs cleanly and both tables show up with data in them.
Every topic points at a level that actually exists.
Running the seed script twice doesn't create duplicate rows.
tickets.verify: npm run db:migrate && npm run db:seed:syllabus && npm run db:studio

tickets.title: Diagnostic question bank: schema and 15 seeded questions
tickets.summary: This is the actual 15-question test. It's written by hand and stored in the database — not generated live — so the test never breaks because an AI service is slow or down.
tickets.why: A test that depends on a third-party API to even load is a fragile thing to demo in front of an examiner. This one doesn't.
tickets.how: One table, diagnostic_questions: id, conceptSlug, difficulty, prompt, options (a list of 4 choices), correctOptionIndex, explanation. Write 15 multiple-choice questions spread across the six concepts — two or three questions per concept, mixing easy and harder ones. Code-writing questions can come later; keep this batch to multiple choice so it's fast to build and fast to grade.
dod: Exactly 15 questions are seeded.
Every correctOptionIndex points at a real option (0 to 3).
Every one of the six concepts has at least one question.
tickets.verify: npm run db:seed:diagnostic && npm run db:studio

tickets.title: Extend onboarding: occupation, experience, language
tickets.summary: Before the diagnostic test starts, the app asks a user what they do, how experienced they are, and what they want to learn. This ticket is the backend side: where those three answers get saved.
tickets.why: The frontend screens in ticket 6 need somewhere real to send this data. Build the landing spot first so that work isn't blocked.
files: src/db/schema.ts (users table, or a new user_profile table)
tickets.how: Add three fields: occupation (plain text), experienceLevel (a fixed set of options — for example Student, Beginner, Some Experience, Experienced), and language (already exists as an enum — for now the only accepted value is Python). Extend the existing POST /me/onboarding endpoint to accept and save all three at once.
dod: Sending all three fields saves them, and fetching the current user shows them back.
Sending an invalid experience level or a non-Python language is rejected with a clear error.
tickets.verify: curl -X POST :3000/me/onboarding \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"occupation":"student","experienceLevel":"BEGINNER","language":"PYTHON"}'

tickets.title: Diagnostic endpoints: serve, grade, and place
tickets.summary: This is the engine room. One endpoint hands out all 15 questions. Another accepts the user's answers all at once, grades them, works out a level, writes it to the database, and tells the frontend where in the syllabus to start.
tickets.why: Everything the user sees on the results screen and the syllabus page comes out of this one ticket.
tickets.how: GET /diagnostic/questions returns all 15 questions — never the correct answers. POST /diagnostic/submit takes the user's answers, grades them against the stored answer key, works out a score out of 15, and picks a level from that score (for example: under 40% Beginner, under 60% Elementary, under 80% Intermediate, otherwise Advanced). It saves an attempt row and calls the AI review service from ticket 5 to write the review text — if that call fails, it must still return a result using the fallback review, never an error. The response includes the score, the level, the review text, which syllabus level to start at, and a breakdown by concept.
dod: The questions endpoint returns exactly 15 questions with no answer key visible.
A perfect score lands on the top level; a zero score lands on the bottom one.
The suggested starting syllabus level always points at a real row.
Submitting still works and returns a result even if the AI service is unreachable.
tickets.verify: curl :3000/diagnostic/questions -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" # then answer them and post to /diagnostic/submit, try both a strong # and a weak set of answers, and try it with the AI key removed

tickets.title: AI review service, with a fallback that never fails
tickets.summary: This writes the two or three sentences of feedback the user reads after the test — something like "you're strong in functions, work on exception handling." It's a separate piece from ticket 4 so it can be tested on its own before it's wired in.
tickets.why: Free-tier AI APIs get rate-limited or slow sometimes. If this ticket only had the AI path, one bad API response could sink a live demo. The fallback text is not a nice-to-have — treat it as equally important as the AI path.
tickets.how: One function, generateReview(score, breakdown, level). It calls whichever free-tier AI provider you're using, asking for a short 2-3 sentence review that names one concept the user did well on and one they should practice, based on the breakdown. Give the call a short timeout (5-8 seconds). If it errors, times out, or the key isn't set, fall back to a template built directly from the breakdown data — for example "You're strongest in {topConcept} and could use more practice with {weakConcept}." That fallback path has to work with zero network calls.
dod: With a working API key, the review mentions a real concept from the breakdown.
With the key removed or invalid, a review still comes back — no crash, no empty response.
tickets.verify: // call generateReview() directly with a sample breakdown, // once with a valid key and once with the key blanked out

tickets.title: Onboarding: the personal-question screens
tickets.summary: Right after signup, before the test, the user answers a couple of quick questions about themselves: what they do, how much coding experience they have, and what they want to learn.
tickets.why: This is the user's first real impression of the product after login — it should feel quick and friendly, not like filling out a form.
tickets.how: Add two new screens before the existing language-pick step: one for occupation (a short pick-list is friendlier than a text box — student, professional, hobbyist), one for experience level (a set of selectable cards). Keep the mascot and progress-dot style already used on the other onboarding screens. Hold all the answers in local state and send them together in one request when the user hits "Start" at the end — don't build a separate network call for each screen.
dod: Every new screen renders and stops the user from continuing until it's answered.
The final submit sends occupation, experience level, and language together, in one request.
tickets.verify: npm run dev # walk through onboarding in the browser, check the Network tab # for a single request carrying all three answers

tickets.title: The 15-question diagnostic player
tickets.summary: The actual test screen. It shows one question at a time out of 15, with a visible sense of progress, and only sends everything to the server once, at the very end.
tickets.why: This is the screen the user spends the most time on. It should feel calm and clear — no surprises about how many questions are left.
tickets.how: Start with a small set of mock questions so this can be built before the backend endpoint (ticket 4) is ready — swap the mock for the real API call in ticket 10. Show one question at a time, a progress indicator like "6 of 15", and collect every answer in local state as the user goes. Only send everything to the server in one batch when they finish the last question, rather than a network call after each answer.
dod: All 15 questions display in order with a visible progress indicator.
The final submit sends every answer in a single request.
tickets.verify: npm run dev # walk through all 15 questions in the browser

tickets.title: The results and review screen
tickets.summary: Right after the test, the user sees their score, their assigned level, the AI-written review, and a button that drops them into the syllabus at the right starting point.
tickets.why: This is the payoff moment — where "I just answered some questions" turns into "here's what I should learn next." Worth making it feel a little rewarding.
tickets.how: Show the score, a level badge, the review text, and a simple per-concept breakdown (reuse whatever chip or list styling already exists on the profile page). One "Start learning" button that takes the user into the syllabus browse page, pre-selecting the level the test recommended.
dod: Every field from the submit response is visible on screen.
The button lands on the syllabus page with the right level pre-selected.
tickets.verify: // finish a diagnostic run and confirm this screen matches // exactly what /diagnostic/submit returned

tickets.title: Syllabus browse page
tickets.summary: The diagnostic result is a starting point, not a cage — the user should be able to look at every level of the syllabus, not just the one they were placed into.
tickets.why: People learn at different speeds. Locking someone to exactly one level would feel restrictive and isn't what was asked for.
tickets.how: List every syllabus level with its topics underneath. Mark the user's recommended starting level with a small "Recommended start" badge, but keep every other level clickable and open too. Clicking a level expands its list of topics.
dod: All levels and their topics load and display from the database.
The recommended level is visually marked but nothing else is locked or disabled.
tickets.verify: // browse the page as a user who has already completed the diagnostic

tickets.title: Wire onboarding, diagnostic, and results to the real backend
tickets.summary: The last step: swap every piece of mock data built in tickets 6, 7, and 8 for real calls to the backend endpoints built in tickets 3 and 4.
tickets.why: This is the ticket that turns five separate working pieces into one working product. Do it last, once the backend tickets have actually landed.
files: Same files touched in tickets 06, 07, and 08
tickets.how: Replace every mock function call with the matching real API call from the contract defined in ticket 4. Use the existing shared API client and error-message pattern for loading and error states — don't invent a new one.
dod: A brand-new registration can walk the whole path — onboarding, diagnostic, results, syllabus — with no mock data left anywhere in it.
tickets.verify: // register a fresh account and walk the entire flow start to finish

tickets.title: Get the backend running: database, migrations, seeds
tickets.summary: Nothing can be demoed until the backend talks to a real database. This ticket gets it working.
tickets.see: Register and login work for real, and the API returns the diagnostic questions and the full syllabus.
tickets.how: Copy the correct connection string from your Supabase dashboard and URL-encode special characters in the password (@ becomes %40). Run the migrations and both seed scripts. Set your AI key and test one real AI review. Push both repos so your teammate has the same code.
dod: Registering a new user works.
A diagnostic submit returns an AI review.
The syllabus endpoint returns all 4 levels.
tickets.verify: curl register, login, /diagnostic/questions and /api/syllabus

tickets.title: Make results match the syllabus, plus a latest-result endpoint
tickets.summary: The diagnostic questions use concept names that don't exist in the syllabus, so results can't link to lessons. This lines them up and adds the endpoints the profile needs.
tickets.see: The results breakdown shows real syllabus concept names, and the profile page can load the user's latest diagnostic.
tickets.how: Rewrite the seed so every question's concept_slug matches a syllabus concept, and make it safe to run twice. Keep 20 questions in the bank but serve exactly 15. Add GET /diagnostic/result (latest attempt, or 404 if none) and PATCH /me for name and language. Make /me return xp and streakCount.
dod: Every diagnostic slug exists in the syllabus.
Running the seed twice doesn't duplicate rows.
/diagnostic/result matches the last submit.
tickets.verify: curl /diagnostic/result after finishing a diagnostic

tickets.title: Lesson endpoint: AI-written lessons, saved and reused
tickets.summary: Writing 160 lessons by hand isn't realistic. The AI writes each lesson the first time someone opens it, and the result is saved so it's instant afterwards.
tickets.see: Opening any concept returns a short lesson with an explanation, a Python example and a common mistake.
tickets.how: Store one lesson per concept. If it exists, return it. Otherwise ask the AI service for a short lesson and save it. If the AI fails, return a simple lesson built from the concept's description without saving it, so a later visit can retry.
dod: The first request generates and saves a lesson.
The second request is instant.
With the key removed, a readable lesson still returns.
tickets.verify: Call the lesson endpoint twice, then once with the AI key removed

tickets.title: Progress, XP and streak endpoints
tickets.summary: Remembers which concepts each user has finished and rewards them.
tickets.see: Completing a concept raises the user's XP and streak, and progress counts show per topic and per level.
tickets.how: One row per user and concept with a status of started or completed. POST /progress/concepts/:id/start, POST /progress/concepts/:id/complete (10 XP, and completing twice must not award XP twice) and GET /progress with completion per topic and level. Streak: add 1 if the last active day was yesterday, keep it if today, otherwise reset to 1.
dod: Completing a concept twice awards XP once.
The streak behaves for today, yesterday and a gap.
GET /progress counts are correct.
tickets.verify: Complete the same concept twice, then check xp on /me

tickets.title: Practice quiz endpoints
tickets.summary: After reading a lesson, the user can test themselves. Questions are AI-generated and saved, with hand-written backups so the demo never breaks.
tickets.see: Each concept has a 5-question practice quiz that is graded and awards bonus XP.
tickets.how: GET /concepts/:id/practice returns 5 multiple-choice questions without the answers. If none are saved, generate and save them with the AI. POST /concepts/:id/practice/submit grades on the server, returns the score with explanations, and awards 5 XP per correct answer. Hand-write 5 backup questions for about 6 concepts and use them if the AI fails.
dod: The questions endpoint never exposes correct answers.
A perfect score awards 25 XP.
With the AI key removed, the backup questions still return for the seeded concepts.
tickets.verify: Fetch questions, submit answers, check the XP on /me

tickets.title: Register to onboarding flow and login routing
tickets.summary: Right now registering ends at a pop-up and users must find the login page themselves.
tickets.see: Signing up drops the user straight into onboarding, real error messages show, and returning users skip the steps they've done.
tickets.how: Create one shared API file with the backend address in an environment variable, and use it in every page instead of the hardcoded address. On register: show the backend's real error text, save the token, go to /onboarding. On login: check /me afterwards and go to onboarding, then the diagnostic, then the syllabus depending on what the user has finished.
dod: A duplicate email shows Email already in use.
Register goes straight into onboarding.
A returning user lands on the syllabus.
tickets.verify: Register a new user, log out, log in again

tickets.title: Profile page with real diagnostic data
tickets.summary: The profile page currently shows fake numbers.
tickets.see: A skill radar, review and breakdown from the user's own diagnostic, editable name and language that stick after refresh, and real XP and streak.
tickets.how: Load /diagnostic/result for the radar, insight and breakdown. Save edits with PATCH /me instead of localStorage. Show real xp and streak. Remove language options the backend doesn't support. Add a Retake diagnostic button.
dod: The radar shows the user's real scores.
An edited name survives a refresh.
No hardcoded XP remains.
tickets.verify: Finish a diagnostic, open /profile, change the name, refresh

tickets.title: Lesson page and live START buttons
tickets.summary: The START buttons on the syllabus do nothing yet.
tickets.see: Clicking START or START TOPIC opens a readable lesson with a code example, and Next and Previous move through the topic.
tickets.how: Wire the START buttons to the lesson page. Render the lesson text with proper code blocks. Add Previous and Next to walk the topic's concepts in order. Show a loading message, because the first open generates the lesson and can take a few seconds.
dod: START opens a real lesson.
Code examples display as code blocks.
Next and Previous follow the topic's order.
tickets.verify: Click START on a Beginner topic and walk through its concepts

tickets.title: Progress, XP header and working sidebar
tickets.summary: Makes progress visible, so the app feels alive.
tickets.see: A Mark complete button on every lesson shows the XP gained, the syllabus shows 3/8 style counts, and an XP and streak bar appears at the top.
tickets.how: Add Mark complete to the lesson page that calls the complete endpoint and shows the XP earned. Use GET /progress to show completion on each topic and level and tick finished concepts. Add a header with xp and streak. Make LEARN and PROFILE real links, and mark PROJECTS and RANKS as Coming soon instead of leaving them silent.
dod: XP and streak update right after completing.
Progress counts match what was finished.
No sidebar item does nothing silently.
tickets.verify: Complete two concepts and watch the counts and XP change

tickets.title: Practice quiz screen
tickets.summary: The most demo-friendly screen: the user tests what they just learned.
tickets.see: A Practice this concept button on each lesson opens a 5-question quiz, then a result screen with the score, explanations and the XP earned.
tickets.how: Reuse the one-question-at-a-time style from the diagnostic player. Fetch the questions, collect answers, submit once, then show the score, which answers were wrong with their explanations, and the bonus XP. Add a Back to lesson and a Next concept button.
dod: The quiz opens from the lesson page.
The result shows score, explanations and XP.
XP in the header updates afterwards.
tickets.verify: Finish a lesson, take its quiz, check the XP
